## Abstract and Figures

Anthropogenic sources, especially industrial, emit into the atmosphere gases and aerosols, which play an important role in atmospheric exchanges. The use of new hyperspectral airborne sensors in the infrared range at high spatial resolution opens the way for further improvements in the characterization of industrial plumes. Existing methods, based on linear or Bayesian approach, present two major limitations: the heterogeneous environment impact on retrievals and the spatial and vertical extents of the plume are not considered. In this paper, a new method for plume characterization is presented to overcome such limitations. This method uses an accurate non linear formalism of cloud gas radiative impact. It includes furthermore a ground classification of the scene, in order to take into account the soil heterogeneity and spectral behaviour. This strategy will be validated using synthetic scenes of industrial area, and real data from Telops Hyper-Cam airborne platform.

ABSTRACT

Anthropogenic sources, especially industrial, emit into the at-

mosphere gases and aerosols, which play an important role

in atmospheric exchanges. The use of new hyperspectral air-

borne sensors in the infrared range at high spatial resolution

opens the way for further improvements in the characteriza-

tion of industrial plumes. Existing methods, based on linear

or Bayesian approach, present two major limitations: the het-

erogeneous environment impact on retrievals and the spatial

and vertical extents of the plume are not considered.

In this paper, a new method for plume characterization is pre-

sented to overcome such limitations. This method uses an

accurate non linear formalism of cloud gas radiative impact.

It includes furthermore a ground classiﬁcation of the scene,

in order to take into account the soil heterogeneity and spec-

tral behaviour. This strategy will be validated using synthetic

scenes of industrial area, and real data from Telops Hyper-

Cam airborne platform.

Index Terms—hyperspectral, plume, gas, thermal in-

1. INTRODUCTION

Anthropogenic sources, especially industrial, are involved

with a major contribution to air pollution. However, these

emissions remain poorly estimated at a high spatial resolu-

tion. Recent technological advances in terms of spatial and

spectral resolutions of thermal infrared airborne hyperspectral

sensors, open a way of improving gaseous efﬂuents charac-

terization, since the majority of gas have their signatures in

the thermal domain.

In literature different approaches were proposed to quan-

tify gaseous efﬂuents using hyperspectral infrared imagery.

Assuming plume gases are optically thin, Young [1] intro-

duces a linear formalism to retrieve plume integrated column

concentration of each pixel. A linear least-squares regression

method is used to determine the thermal contrast, which is di-

rectly related to the integrated column concentration.

Heasler, et al. [2] follow a Bayesian approach. They devel-

oped a non-linear regression using the Metropolis-Hastings

algorithm. The atmospheric terms are supposed to be known.

As the background clutter (ground temperature and emissiv-

ity) is the dominant source of variability, it is handled as nui-

sance parameters.

A previous study [3] showed some of the limitations of

such characterization methods. First, the spatial and vertical

extents of the plume are not taken into account in these meth-

ods, which induces a miscalculation of the plume radiative

impact. Then, the heterogeneous environment of an indus-

trial scene impact a lot on the retrieval performances of these

methods [4].

Hereinafter, we present a new method of plume characteriza-

tion, which takes into account the vertical extent of the plume.

Moreover, our retrieval is preceded by a classiﬁcation of the

background, in order to deal with soil heterogeneity.

The paper is organized in the following way: section 2 is ded-

icated to the description of the plume retrieval methodology.

Then, sections 3 and 4 evaluate the application of our method

on synthetic data and Telops Hyper-Cam airborne platform

data.

3.2. Initial guess

The CONLIE is initialized using a pixel-to-pixel linear in-

version method [1]. The latter takes as input the differential

radiance ∆L through the scene. After an estimation of the

plume temperature of each pixel using the absorbtion bands

of the water vapor, a linear least-squares regression gives us

the integrated column concentration (Fig. 3). We notice that

the retrieved concentrations are close to those simulated, for

pixels far from the emission source. 
The next step in our work is to introduce a more realistic spa-

tial constraint on this image. Moreover, we should to test

CONLIE on real images that need the use of both spatial and

vertical constraints.
